E0406.summary: Atwood's term for the ground where the Scriptural phrase is seen and proved; there man may work but cannot compel the Divine Blessing.
E0406.body: Atwood speaks of what is “as seen and proved on the Divine Ground” [IV.1 ¶40]. On this ground, she says, man may experiment, plough, plant and irrigate, but he cannot compel the Divine Blessing [IV.1 ¶40].

E0407.summary: The affirmation in which Life feels itself to Be; Atwood says the Kabalah uses it to signify the Substant Unity of all that is.
E0407.body: In Atwood's account, “Life springs forth with motion, feeling itself to Be.” [III.3 ¶79]. She identifies the Divine I Am with the Substant Unity: “in the Divine I Am, is by the Kabalah signified the Substant Unity of all that is” [III.3 ¶79].

E0408.summary: What, according to Atwood, those who live profanely and without self-knowledge cannot attain, entertain or think self-actively.
E0408.body: Atwood says that those living profanely and without self-knowledge cannot “attain to the Divine Idea; either to entertain or think It self-actively is impossible” [III.3 ¶78].

E0409.summary: In Boehme as quoted, that through which all things arose from the Tincture.
E0409.body: Quoted from Boehme: “All things are thence arisen through the Divine Imagination” [III.2 ¶16]. The context ties this arising to the Tincture [III.2 ¶16].

E0410.summary: Atwood's name for the passive reception of the divine, raised by love, hope and faith, as opposed to self-active comprehension of Deity.
E0410.body: Atwood contrasts “the passive method of the Divine Intuition” [II.4 ¶40] with a self-active comprehension of Deity. In this mode the divine is received passively, and the soul is raised by love, hope and faith [II.4 ¶40].

E0411.summary: A term Atwood names as the subject of a Rabbi's advice and links to creation out of nothing, but does not define.
E0411.body: Atwood refers to advice “concerning the true nature of Divine Inversion” [III.2 ¶31] and connects it with creation out of nothing. The passage does not define the term.

E0412.summary: The formless divine light that the initiate sees; Atwood says it is held captive in this life and that it turns the Quintessence into living gold. In the Appendix she calls it the Essence of Gold.
E0412.body:
**Quoted (Psellus; the Oracle).** In the Introspection, “the initiated person sees the Divine Light itself without any form or figure” [II.3 ¶46]. The oracle calls this Sacro Sancto [II.3 ¶46], and speaks of it: “When thou seest a Fire without Form” [II.3 ¶47]; this light, the quoted voices say, will not deceive.

**Atwood.** Without this revelation the operator's purpose is blind. She warns against “he who presumes without the revelation of the Divine Light to introduce his own blind purpose” [III.1 ¶38]. The new life “needs only the corroborative virtue of the Divine light which it draws” [III.1 ¶49], and this turns the Quintessence into living gold. ¶40 also mentions a guardian of the Light [III.1 ¶40]. In this life the light is kept behind “the barriers by which the Divine Light is here held in thralldom” [IV.4 ¶17], and the means of the ancients remove those barriers. “When once the Divine Light is loosened in life” [IV.3 ¶39], everything prospers so long as her Rule is kept; the text leaves unclear whether “her” means the Light or Wisdom.

**Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer).** Atwood says the Divine Light is hidden in the self-begotten life, which takes the Divine Life for itself instead of serving it. She identifies it with gold: “The Divine Light, the Essence of Gold” [APP ¶70].

E0413.summary: In the Appendix, the highest sphere, above the pure Ether, where high Reason dwells, informed by Love and purified by humiliation.
E0413.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes a scale of spheres: “Above that is the Divine Light region” [APP ¶170]. It lies above the pure Ether and is the dwelling of high Reason, informed by Love and purified by humiliation [APP ¶170].

E0414.summary: The real means by which, Atwood says, Theurgists are joined to the Divine nature, as opposed to a mental conception.
E0414.body: Atwood insists that the Theurgists' union with the Divine nature is real: “it is indeed by divine Media, and not a mere conception of the mind or metaphysical abstraction” [II.4 ¶31].

E0415.summary: Something Atwood says is established from the triune-essence principles she has just set out.
E0415.body: After her passage on the triune essence, Atwood writes: “Hence the Divine Monarchy consists, and is established” [IV.2 ¶12]. Its primary principles are those she has just announced there.

E0416.summary: An oracular voice Atwood cites as ratifying the Platonic instruction on how to apprehend the Intelligible.
E0416.body: Atwood cites the Divine Oracle in support of the Platonic teaching on how to apprehend the Intelligible: “There is something Intelligible which it behooves thee to understand with the Flower of thy mind.” [II.4 ¶42]. The citation continues across [II.4 ¶43–48]. She uses it approvingly.

E0417.summary: Oracles Atwood cites as teaching that fire obliterates the strains from generation.
E0417.body: In a footnote, Atwood cites the divine oracles in support: they teach that fire obliterates the strains from generation [II.3 n40].

E0418.summary: The divine source in which contraries always coexist; Atwood says the common elements of Nature hide it and chemistry cannot identify it.
E0418.body: Atwood says that “contraries are always consubsistent in the Divine Original” [III.2 ¶60], such as small and great, deficient and exceeding. Elsewhere she writes: “The common elements of Nature obscure their Divine Original” [IV.1 ¶47]. In that context, chemistry cannot identify this source [IV.1 ¶47].

E0419.summary: A principle said to have been originally resident in man's life, which ranked him high, reported from cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience.
E0419.body: Reporting cabalistic scriptures and schools of antique experience, Atwood describes man as ranked high for “a Divine Reason, on occult principle of Causal Efficience, said to be originally resident in his life” [II.1 ¶32]. This passage identifies the Divine Reason with that occult principle of Causal Efficience.

E0420.summary: The knowledge whose temple, Atwood says, admits whoever knows the first entrance and the volatilizing.
E0420.body: Atwood says that whoever knows the first entrance and the volatilizing “is already admitted to the temple of Divine Science, and joins in with the whole conclave” [IV.4 ¶32].

E0421.summary: What the matter brought into the right condition attracts, and (in the Appendix) what the spirit that has died to all receives.
E0421.body: In the main text, the matter is brought into the right condition by action and reaction, so as “to supply the right condition for attracting the Divine Seed” [IV.1 ¶41]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the spirit dies to everything, even its own identity, and becomes “a simple receptacle and magnet for the Divine Seed” [APP ¶87]. Both passages describe a prepared receiver that draws in the Seed.

E0422.summary: In Trismegistus as quoted, the knowledge of the First Cause: a rest of all the senses in which the soul is changed into the Essence of God.
E0422.body: Atwood quotes Trismegistus on the First Cause: “the knowledge of it, says Trismegistus, is a most Divine Silence, and a rest of all the senses” [IV.2 ¶33]. In this state the soul is drawn from the body and changed into the Essence of God [IV.2 ¶33].

E0423.summary: In the theosophist as quoted, the pure spirit that nourished the flame-like life of Adam before the fall.
E0423.body: The theosophist, as quoted, says that unfallen Adam's flame-like life was “nourished by that pure spirit of the divine substantiality” [IV.3 ¶38].

E0424.summary: Atwood's name for the completed work; the returned Instrument gives it its force and integral perfection.
E0424.body: Atwood says the returned Instrument makes up “the force and integral perfection of the Divine Superstructure” [III.1 ¶61]. The term apparently names the finished work.

E0425.summary: Cited from the Scriptures to support keeping the Causal Knowledge from the unworthy.
E0425.body: Atwood cites the Divine Teacher of the Scriptures to justify withholding the Causal Knowledge from the unworthy: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine” [I.3 n10]. She uses it with approval.

E0426.summary: Union with the reality that images stand for. Julian, as quoted, says it is achieved only with the help of Divine Works.
E0426.body:
**Quoted (Julian).** “without such assistance the Divine union is neither effected not rightly understood” [II.1 ¶52]. The assistance meant here is Divine Works.

**Atwood.** Divine Union joins the soul not to an image but to the reality that images represent. Afterwards, what was in the mind before returns heightened: “subsequent to the Divine Union, there recurs That also which was in the mind prior to the union, exalted and multiplied” [III.2 ¶66].

E0427.summary: In Hermolaus Barbarus as quoted, the chemists' celestial water, an ethereal spirit from which potable gold and the philosophers' stone begin.
E0427.body: Quoted from Hermolaus Barbarus: “There is a celestial, or rather a divine water of the chemists” [I.1 ¶20]. It is distinct from every other water or liquor, and Democritus and Trismegistus knew it. It is called by other names, “calling it divine water, Scythian latex, &c.” [I.1 ¶20]. He calls it a spirit “which is a spirit of the nature of the ether and quintessence of things” [I.1 ¶20]. Potable gold and the philosophers' stone begin from it. If the outside air is kept out, its ether burns forever: “concerning this water; and he devoutly affirms, that the ether in this praeter-perfect aqueous body will burn perpetually” [I.1 ¶20].

E0428.summary: In Synesius as quoted, the help without which the Divine union can neither be achieved nor understood.
E0428.body: Synesius, as cited, “bears witness to the efficacy of Divine Works” [II.1 ¶52]. Without this help the Divine union is neither effected nor understood [II.1 ¶52].

E0429.summary: The Greeks' teaching, which Atwood praises as unequalled in its scientific explanation of the divine source.
E0429.body: Atwood praises the Greeks as unequalled in “their doctrine of Wisdom in perspicuity, grace of utterance, and scientific explication of the divine source” [I.1 ¶70].

E0430.summary: In Vaughan as quoted, a twofold birth, visible and invisible, without which the Matter cannot be brought to its final purpose.
E0430.body: Vaughan, as quoted, speaks “of a double nativity, visible and invisible” [IV.2 ¶35]. Without it the Matter cannot be altered to its final purpose. The passage does not explain the expression further.

E0431.summary: In Eirenaeus as quoted, a sign to watch for; the passage does not explain it.
E0431.body: Eirenaeus, as quoted, names “your signal the Doves of Diana” [III.1 ¶14]. The passage does not say what they are.

E0432.summary: In the Appendix, Atwood's gloss for the maternal instinct, through which the light finds the Paternal Life.
E0432.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood explains the term herself: the light finds the Paternal Life “through the maternal instinct (the doves of Venus)” [APP ¶167]. Her stated meaning is the maternal instinct.

E0433.summary: In Proclus as quoted, what belongs to opinion: uncertain, close to irrational life, and not true discovery.
E0433.body: Quoting Proclus, Atwood separates true discovery from what is “not that which is doxastic, or pertaining to opinion” [II.4 ¶41]. Such opinion is uncertain and close to irrational life [II.4 ¶41].

E0434.summary: Translator of the Hermetic books into English; Atwood praises the translation.
E0434.body: Atwood praises Dr Everard's English translation of the Hermetic books [I.1 ¶7].

E0435.summary: For Atwood, the self-willed spirit that came into nature with the fall into generation and appears as the matter's blackness; Hermes, Bloomfield and a French adept, as quoted, describe it differently.
E0435.body:
**Atwood.** In her own words: “The dragon is the self-willed spirit” [I.3 n31]. It entered nature through the fall into generation. It lives in water, oily tincture and faeces, and it rises through blackness. It is the matter's blackness at the first ascension. It is poisonous: “like a poisonous dragon it destroys all that it touches” [I.3 n31]. It watches the crevices and shuns the sunbeams. As the internal light rises, the dragon is hidden: it “becomes so occultated in the rising of the internal light to manifestation” [I.3 n43]. The Dragon therefore apparently marks the dark first stage, which gives way as the light appears.

**Quoted (Hermes).** “The Dragon dwells in all the threefold nature, and his houses are the darkness and blackness that is in them” [III.1 ¶61]. In the same passage, the French adept describes two dragons biting each other until they become a Fifth Essence [III.1 ¶61].

**Quoted (Bloomfield).** The Dragon is the first of the three, and it slays and quells the other two: “The first one is the Dragon fell” [IV.2 ¶36].

The sources don't agree on the details. Atwood treats the Dragon as the self-willed spirit and the blackness, Hermes as a principle dwelling in the threefold nature, and Bloomfield as the first of three, which overcomes the others.
